title: Judge Limits Government Search for Noncitizens on Voter Lists
summary:
With the midterm elections less than two weeks away, a federal judge in California has put limits on a U.S. government effort to look for noncitizens on voter lists.

Voter lists, also called voter rolls, are records of people who are registered to vote. In the United States, only citizens may vote in federal elections. Voting by noncitizens is already illegal, and reporters note that it is extremely rare.

According to a lawsuit, the Department of Homeland Security, or DHS, has been running an operation since August that it calls the Unlawful Voter Initiative. Hundreds of DHS agents have been assigned to look for voter fraud.

The judge ruled that DHS must restrict its field work. Agents cannot stop people for interviews unless they believe a person is a noncitizen. The ruling covers nine states: California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The judge was concerned that lists made by DHS contained errors and included the names of citizens. The order was set to start a day later, giving the government time to appeal.

In a separate case, the Department of Justice says about 20,000 noncitizens are on voter rolls in California. California officials, including the Los Angeles County registrar, say they do not know whether that list is accurate, because it was built from incomplete state data. The registrar's office said it has not stopped processing mail ballots. Another court hearing is set for next Tuesday.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said, "We're not trying to create chaos." Meanwhile, a group of Democratic organizations has sued the Trump administration, saying the actions amount to voter intimidation.

The cases show how courts help decide the rules for elections when people disagree.
why_it_matters: Fair elections depend on accurate voter lists and on voters feeling free to vote, so courts are deciding how far the federal government can go in checking eligibility right before a national election.

background_read: In the United States, people must be citizens to vote in federal elections, and states keep lists of registered voters called voter rolls.
The Department of Homeland Security is a federal agency that handles border, immigration and security work, while the Department of Justice enforces federal laws in court.
When people or groups think a government action breaks the law, they can file a lawsuit, and a judge can order the government to stop or limit what it is doing.
Because the midterm elections are close, courts are deciding quickly how far these federal checks on voters may go.
